title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Sacroiliac joint (SIJ) pain represents a frequently underrecognized source of low back pain, accounting for up to one quarter of mechanical cases. Clinical presentation often overlaps with lumbar spine, hip, and radicular disorders, complicating diagnosis across specialties. Etiologies include degenerative change, inflammatory arthritis, pregnancy-related ligamentous laxity, trauma, leg length discrepancy, and prior spinal surgery. Pain typically manifests as persistent axial low back discomfort, sometimes radiating to the buttock or posterior thigh. Diagnostic uncertainty arises from anatomic variability and limited joint space, which challenge both physical examination and imaging correlation. Untreated or misdiagnosed SIJ dysfunction may prolong disability and delay appropriate management.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity enhances clinician competence in evaluating and managing suspected SIJ-mediated pain through image-guided injection. Participants review relevant anatomy, biomechanics, indications, contraindications, patient selection, preparation, equipment, technique, and potential complications. Emphasis is placed on fluoroscopic or ultrasound-guided intra-articular needle placement for diagnostic confirmation and short-term therapeutic relief. Collaboration with an interprofessional team, including pain specialists, radiology professionals, physical therapists, and nursing staff, strengthens diagnostic accuracy, procedural safety, and longitudinal care planning. Coordinated management supports timely intervention, reduces complications, and improves functional outcomes in individuals with low back pain.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Introduction
content: Sacroiliac joint (SIJ) pain is a common contributor to mechanical low back pain, accounting for approximately 10% to 27% of cases. [1] [2] Pain may refer to the buttocks, groin, or lower extremities. SIJ dysfunction can result from degenerative changes, altered pelvic biomechanics, trauma, inflammatory arthropathies, pregnancy, or prior lumbar spine surgery. [3] [4] [5] Diagnosis is challenging due to symptom overlap with lumbar spine and hip pathology. Clinical suspicion is raised through characteristic pain patterns and reproduction of symptoms with provocative maneuvers. Image-guided SIJ injection serves both as a diagnostic block, confirming the SIJ as the pain generator, and a therapeutic intervention to reduce pain and facilitate rehabilitation.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The SIJs are paired diarthrodial–amphiarthrodial articulations between the sacrum and ilium. The auricular surfaces of these joints are stabilized by a robust ligamentous complex, including the interosseous, anterior, and posterior sacroiliac ligaments, as well as the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments. The primary function of the SIJs is to provide pelvic stability and attenuate forces transmitted between the lower extremities and the spine (see Image . Ligamentous Connections of the Human Pelvis).

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Despite this stabilizing role, the SIJs demonstrate limited motion, averaging 2° to 4° of rotation and 1 to 2 mm of translation. [6] Motion includes anterior and posterior innominate tilt, as well as sacral nutation and counternutation relative to the ilium. During nutation, the sacrum moves anteriorly and inferiorly. Counternutation involves posterior and superior movement of the sacrum. SIJ innervation is variable and incompletely defined, but sensory input is generally attributed to the lateral branches of the dorsal rami from L5 through S4. [7] This innervation pattern explains variable pain referral and supports the rationale for lateral branch radiofrequency ablation in selected patients.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Indications
content: SIJ injection is indicated for diagnostic confirmation and therapeutic management of suspected SIJ-mediated pain. A diagnostic block confirms the SIJ as the pain generator when the symptom decreases by at least 75% during the expected anesthetic duration with previously painful activities. [8] Diagnostic indications include axial low back pain localized below L5, reproduction of pain with 3 or more SIJ provocative maneuvers (eg, FABER, Gaenslen, compression, distraction, thigh thrust), and failure to identify an alternative primary pain source. Therapeutic indications include confirmed refractoriness of SIJ pain to conservative interventions, such as activity modification, physical therapy, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug treatment, inflammatory sacroiliitis, and functional rehabilitation requiring adjunctive pain control.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Contraindications
content: Absolute contraindications to SIJ injection include known hypersensitivity to injectates, local malignancy at the injection site, and active infection involving the SIJ. Relative contraindications include coagulopathy or ongoing anticoagulant therapy, pregnancy requiring a risk–benefit assessment, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, and other infectious conditions, including systemic infection, septic joint, or osteomyelitis.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Equipment
content: All equipment and materials for SIJ injection should be organized and checked prior to the procedure. Supplies required for SIJ injection include the following: Fluoroscopic C-arm or computed tomography scanner for image-guided needle placement Sterile gloves and antiseptic solution for skin preparation (eg, povidone-iodine) Sterile procedural tray with draping materials Local anesthetic agents (eg, lidocaine or bupivacaine) Corticosteroid medications (eg, triamcinolone, methylprednisolone, or dexamethasone) Nonionic contrast medium to confirm intra-articular needle placement 22- to 25-gauge spinal needle, typically 3.5 to 5 inches in length

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Personnel
content: All personnel involved in SIJ injection should be trained in sterile technique, fluoroscopic or CT navigation, and management of procedural complications. Key personnel include the procedural clinician (eg, orthopedic surgeon, pain specialist, or radiologist), a procedural assistant, and a radiologic technologist.

content: Informed consent must be obtained, including discussion of risks, benefits, and alternatives. A procedural time-out confirms patient identity and the correct injection site. The patient is positioned prone with appropriate padding to optimize access and comfort.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Technique or Treatment -- Fluoroscopy-Guided Injection
content: According to practice guidelines from the International Spine Intervention Society, the patient is positioned prone with a pillow under the abdomen at the level of the iliac crests to reduce lumbar lordosis. The fluoroscopic C-arm is initially positioned in an anteroposterior orientation and adjusted with slight obliquity until the inferior portion of the SIJ is clearly visualized. An optimal image is achieved when the bony margins of the inferior joint space appear parallel.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Technique or Treatment -- Fluoroscopy-Guided Injection
content: Once the target site is identified, the skin is marked, prepped, and draped in a sterile fashion (see Image . Fast-Find Grid). Under intermittent fluoroscopic guidance, a spinal needle is advanced into the inferior portion of the SIJ. Entry into the joint may be accompanied by a subtle loss of resistance or tactile “pop.” After confirming appropriate needle placement, 0.3 to 0.5 mL of contrast is injected (see Image . Sacroiliac Joint Injection). Intra-articular placement is confirmed when the contrast outlines the SIJ without vascular uptake. Although the ideal injectate volume remains debated, injection is typically limited by a firm endpoint, evidence of extracapsular spread, or a maximum total volume of 2.5 mL.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Technique or Treatment -- Computed Tomography–Guided Injection
content: CT-guided SIJ injection is performed with the patient in a prone position. An initial CT scan identifies the most direct and safe trajectory to the inferior-posterior aspect of the SIJ. The skin entry site is marked, followed by sterile preparation and draping. Local anesthesia is administered, typically using approximately 5 mL of 1% lidocaine. Under CT guidance, a 22-gauge spinal needle is advanced into the targeted joint space. The injectate is delivered after satisfactory needle placement is confirmed. The needle is withdrawn, and hemostasis is achieved with manual compression.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Complications
content: SIJ injections are generally safe when performed with image guidance. Most adverse effects are minor and include postprocedural soreness, transient pain flare, and vasovagal reaction. [9] [10] Uncommon but more serious complications include nerve injury or unintended nerve root block, hematoma, infection (including septic sacroiliitis), intravascular injection, and steroid-related systemic effects. [11] [12]

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Clinical Significance
content: SIJ injections are used for both diagnosis and treatment when SIJ-mediated pain is suspected. Blind injection techniques demonstrate poor accuracy, with intra-articular needle placement achieved in only 12% to 22% of cases, underscoring the need for image guidance for diagnostic validity and procedural safety. [13] [14] Fluoroscopy allows real-time confirmation of intra-articular contrast spread and visualization of injectate distribution, whereas CT provides superior anatomic detail and the highest accuracy for needle placement. Ultrasound guidance is more operator-dependent and less effective at confirming intra-articular delivery. [15]

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Clinical Significance
content: Systematic reviews support the relative safety and effectiveness of corticosteroid use in SIJ injections. [16] [17] Evidence demonstrates moderate support for SIJ injections in chronic LBP and referred pain below L5. Therapeutic injections may provide sustained relief in selected patients, with results from several studies showing pain reduction lasting longer than 6 weeks in approximately two-thirds of patients with spondyloarthropathy and a mean duration of benefit approaching 37 weeks among responders. [18] Meta-analyses report fair evidence supporting the use of therapeutic SIJ injections. [19] Alternative interventions, such as lateral branch radiofrequency ablation or minimally invasive SIJ fusion, may be considered when symptom relief is inadequate.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective evaluation and management of SIJ-mediated pain requires coordinated interprofessional collaboration across the continuum of care. SIJ injections are commonly performed by orthopedic surgeons, sports medicine clinicians, pain specialists, and radiologists, with support from nursing staff and radiologic technologists to ensure procedural accuracy, patient safety, and appropriate postprocedure monitoring. Accurate diagnosis depends on shared clinical assessment, consistent use of provocative testing, and appropriate imaging to confirm the SIJ as the pain generator. Image-guided techniques and standardized procedural protocols enhance diagnostic reliability and treatment effectiveness.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Collaboration among physical therapists, advanced practice clinicians, and nurses is critical for patient education, rehabilitation, and longitudinal care. Physical therapists restore mobility and address biomechanical contributors to SIJ dysfunction, while nurses reinforce postprocedural instructions and monitor for complications. Clear communication regarding diagnostic findings, treatment response, and follow-up planning supports continuity of care and reduces unnecessary interventions. Participation in this interprofessional educational activity promotes coordinated decision-making and evidence-based practice, resulting in safer care, improved functional outcomes, and higher-quality pain management for patients with SIJ-related pain.
